For a prime \(p\) let  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\min\{\,k\ge 1 : a^{k}\equiv 1\pmod p\,\}.
\]

Because the multiplicative group \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) is cyclic,
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\mid p-1\) for every \(a\not\equiv 0\pmod p\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 1.  What \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) tends to

For a fixed prime \(p\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q\!\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\bigr)}\;
\prod_{q>x} q^{v_q(p-1)} .
\]

If \(x\to\infty\) the second product disappears, hence  

\[
\lim_{x\to\infty}\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a).
\]

Consequently  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x=
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}}
{\#\{p\le t\}} .
\]

Thus \(d_{\infty}\) is the natural density of the set  

\[
S:=\{p\text{ prime }:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  Symmetry between the two numbers

For a fixed prime \(p\) the two events  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3),\qquad
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)
\]

have the same probability, because the map  

\[
a\longmapsto a^{-1}\pmod p
\]

is a bijection of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) that interchanges the
orders of \(2\) and \(3\).  Hence

\[
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\bigr)
=
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\bigr).
\]

Let  

\[
E=\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}.
\]

Then for every prime \(p\),

\[
\mathbf 1_{S}(p)+\mathbf 1_{S^{c}}(p)+\mathbf 1_{E}(p)=1,
\]

where \(S^{c}\) denotes the set \(\{p:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)\}\).
Taking densities and using the symmetry gives  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-\delta(E)}{2},
\tag{1}
\]

where \(\displaystyle\delta(E)=\lim_{t\to\infty}
\frac{\#\{p\le t:p\in E\}}{\#\{p\le t\}}\) (if it exists).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 3.  The set where the two orders are equal has density 0

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
2\in\langle 3\rangle\subset (\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}
\Longleftrightarrow
\exists k\ge 1:\; 2\equiv 3^{\,k}\pmod p .
\]

Thus every prime in \(E\) divides a number of the form  

\[
2-3^{k}\qquad(k=1,2,\dots ).
\]

For a fixed \(k\) the integer \(2-3^{k}\) has only finitely many prime
divisors; consequently the set  

\[
\bigcup_{k\ge 1}\{\,p\mid p\mid 2-3^{k}\,\}
\]

is a countable union of finite sets, hence it has natural density \(0\).
Therefore  

\[
\delta(E)=0 .
\tag{2}
\]

(One can also view this as a special case of a general result: the set of
primes for which two fixed non‑zero integers generate the same cyclic
subgroup of \((\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^{\times}\) has Dirichlet density \(0\).)

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 4.  Computing \(d_{\infty}\)

Putting (2) into (1) we obtain  

\[
d_{\infty}= \frac{1-0}{2}= \frac12 .
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 5.  Required integer

\[
\bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\,d_{\infty}\bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 10^{6}\times \tfrac12 \bigr\rfloor
= \bigl\lfloor 500\,000 \bigr\rfloor
= 500\,000 .
\]

The density \(d_{\infty}\) is the proportion of primes \(p\) for which the (full) multiplicative order of \(2\) modulo \(p\) exceeds that of \(3\).
For a large \(x\) the truncated order \(\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)\) coincides with the true order \(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\); hence  

\[
d_{\infty}= \lim_{x\to\infty} d_x = 
\lim_{t\to\infty}\frac{\#\{p\le t:\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\}}
{\pi(t)} .
\]

---

### 1.  Distribution of the orders

For a prime \(p\) the multiplicative group \((\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z})^{\times}\) is cyclic of order \(p-1\).
If \(g\) is a generator, any non‑zero residue \(a\) can be written as \(a\equiv g^{t}\pmod p\) with
\(t\in\{0,\dots ,p-2\}\).  
The order of \(a\) is  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)=\frac{p-1}{\gcd(p-1,t)} .
\]

Heuristically the exponent \(t\) behaves like a uniformly random element of
\(\mathbb Z/(p-1)\mathbb Z\).  
Consequently the probability that a given prime divisor \(\ell\) of \(p-1\) divides
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(a)\) is \(\displaystyle 1-\frac{1}{\ell}\); the
probability that \(\ell\) does **not** divide the order is \(1/\ell\).
In particular the probability that the order equals the maximal possible value
\(p-1\) (i.e. that \(a\) is a primitive root) is the Artin constant

\[
A = 0.3739558136\ldots .
\]

If \(a\) is divisible by an odd prime \(q\) (here \(a=3\) is divisible by \(3\)),
the primitive‑root density is multiplied by the factor \((1-\frac{1}{q-1})\).
Thus

\[
\begin{aligned}
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)=p-1\bigr) &= A,\\[2mm]
\Pr\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)=p-1\bigr) &= A\Bigl(1-\frac{1}{3-1}\Bigr)=\frac{A}{2}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For all other possible orders we assume the same distribution for the two
integers, and, conditioned on “neither is a primitive root”, the orders are
symmetrically distributed; consequently each of the two possibilities
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_{p}(2)<\operatorname{ord}_{p}(3)\) occurs with probability
\(1/2\).

---

### 2.  Computing the density

Let  

\[
\begin{aligned}
P_2 &= A, \qquad &P_3 &= \frac{A}{2},\\
\bar P_2 &= 1-P_2, \qquad &\bar P_3 &= 1-P_3 .
\end{aligned}
\]

The required density is

\[
\begin{aligned}
d_{\infty}
&= \underbrace{P_2\bar P_3}_{\text{2 primitive, 3 not}}
   \;+\;
   \underbrace{\frac12\,\bar P_2\bar P_3}_{\text{neither primitive, symmetry}}\\[2mm]
&= A\Bigl(1-\frac{A}{2}\Bigr)
   +\frac12\Bigl(1-A\Bigr)\Bigl(1-\frac{A}{2}\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

Insert the numerical value of \(A\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
A &= 0.3739558136,\\
1-\frac{A}{2} &= 0.8130220932,\\[1mm]
d_{\infty}
&= 0.3739558136\cdot0.8130220932
   +\frac12\,(0.6260441864)\cdot0.8130220932\\
&\approx 0.3040343387 + 0.2544938774\\
&\approx 0.5585282161.
\end{aligned}
\]

Let's present reasoning.

The definition  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}
                     \prod_{q> x} q^{v_q(p-1)}
\]

replaces, for the “large’’ primes \(q>x\), the exponent of \(q\) in
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\) by the (larger) exponent of \(q\) in \(p-1\).
Because \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)\mid p-1\) we have  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(a)=\operatorname{ord}_p(a)
        \prod_{q>x} q^{\,v_q(p-1)-v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(a))}\; .
\]

Hence the factor contributed by the primes \(q>x\) is the same for
\(a=2\) and for \(a=3\).  Consequently  

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow
\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(2))}
   >\prod_{q\le x} q^{v_q(\operatorname{ord}_p(3))}.
\]

When \(x\) exceeds the largest prime divisor of \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\)
and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) the two products become the whole orders,
so for sufficiently large \(x\)

\[
\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(2)>\operatorname{ord}_{p,x}(3)
\Longleftrightarrow \operatorname{ord}_p(2)>\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

Therefore  

\[
d_\infty=\lim_{x\to\infty} d_x
   =\text{density of primes }p\text{ with }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
     \operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

### 1.  Reducing to a symmetry problem  

For a given prime \(p\) the two orders \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)\) and
\(\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) are divisors of \(p-1\).  Apart from the
possibility that they are equal, the situation \(\operatorname{ord}_p(2)>
\operatorname{ord}_p(3)\) is symmetric to the opposite inequality.
Hence  

\[
d_\infty=\frac{1-\delta}{2},
\]

where  

\[
\delta=\text{density of primes for which }\operatorname{ord}_p(2)
       =\operatorname{ord}_p(3).
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
### 2.  When can the two orders be equal?  

The equality can occur only when both \(2\) and \(3\) have the same
order \(d\) dividing \(p-1\).  The most common case is \(d=p-1\); i.e.
both numbers are primitive roots modulo \(p\).

For a fixed integer \(a\) that is not a perfect power, Artin’s conjecture
(and its proof under GRH) states that the set of primes for which
\(a\) is a primitive root has a positive density

\[
A=\prod_{q\ \text{prime}}\Bigl(1-\frac1{q(q-1)}\Bigr)
      =0.373\,955\,8136\ldots
\]

(the same constant for every such \(a\)).  Assuming the natural
independence of the two conditions “\(2\) is a primitive root’’ and
“\(3\) is a primitive root’’ (the corresponding splitting fields are
linearly disjoint), the density of primes for which **both** are primitive
roots is the product

\[
\delta_0 = A^2 .
\]

Primes for which the two orders are equal to a proper divisor of
\(p-1\) contribute a negligible amount to the density (their expected
frequency is of order \(1/\log p\)).  Hence we may take  

\[
\delta = A^{2}.
\]

\[
\begin{aligned}
A &= 0.373\,955\,8136\ldots ,\\[2mm]
\delta &= A^{2}=0.373\,955\,8136^{2}=0.139\,842\ldots ,\\[2mm]
d_\infty &=\frac{1-\delta}{2}
          =\frac{1-0.139\,842\ldots}{2}
          =0.430\,078\ldots .
\end{aligned}
\]
